blocks.text: Many scholars date Matthew roughly 70–100 CE, often after Jerusalem’s temple destruction, though the text itself gives no exact year. The chapter brings together the temple’s destruction, tribulation, the coming of the Son of Man, uncertainty about timing, readiness, stewardship, and judgment; readers should avoid reducing all these themes to a single timetable.

Jesus’ reference to the “abomination of desolation” in verse 15 draws on Danielic imagery. Daniel’s desolating-abomination language has an earlier temple-desecration horizon and was reused in later Jewish and Christian settings. Since the Synoptic Gospels and Revelation also reuse Daniel’s imagery in new literary settings, each use needs to be interpreted in its own setting rather than treated as automatically identical.
Verse 36 explicitly denies that anyone knows the day or hour. Matthew 24 therefore cannot legitimately be used to set apocalyptic dates.
